```{r}
#| label: setup-plot-style
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(showtext)   # install.packages("showtext")

# slide fonts (downloaded from Google Fonts at render time)
font_add_google("Ubuntu", "ubuntu", regular.wt = 300, bold.wt = 500)
font_add_google("Roboto Slab", "robotoslab", regular.wt = 300, bold.wt = 700)
font_add_google("Yanone Kaffeesatz", "yanone", regular.wt = 400, bold.wt = 700)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.showtext = TRUE)

# slide colors (econpol_slides.scss)
pal <- c(blue = "#5d8198", red = "#e76254", dred = "#d03161", yellow = "#ffd500",
         green = "#218500", brown = "#d37b00",
         grey200 = "#e9ecef", grey400 = "#ced4da", grey500 = "#adb5bd",
         grey600 = "#868e96", grey800 = "#343a40", grey900 = "#212529")

# ordered palette from blue to red, for many ordered categories
pal_ramp <- function(n) colorRampPalette(c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["red"]]))(n)

# ggplot theme matching the slides:
# Ubuntu for text, Roboto Slab for numbers, Yanone Kaffeesatz in red for titles
theme_econpol <- function(base_size = 12,
                          text_x = TRUE, text_y = TRUE,      # axis text (tick labels)
                          title_x = TRUE, title_y = TRUE) {  # axis titles
  th <- theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "ubuntu") +
    theme(
      text          = element_text(colour = pal[["grey800"]]),
      panel.grid    = element_blank(),
      axis.text     = element_text(family = "robotoslab", colour = pal[["grey600"]],
                                   size = rel(0.85)),
      axis.title.x  = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
      axis.title.y  = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
      plot.title    = element_text(family = "yanone", colour = pal[["red"]],
                                   size = rel(1.8), margin = margin(b = 6)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = pal[["grey600"]]),
      plot.caption  = element_text(family = "robotoslab", colour = pal[["grey600"]],
                                   size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title    = element_blank(),
      legend.key.width = unit(1, "null")
    )
  if (!text_x)  th <- th + theme(axis.text.x  = element_blank())
  if (!text_y)  th <- th + theme(axis.text.y  = element_blank())
  if (!title_x) th <- th + theme(axis.title.x = element_blank())
  if (!title_y) th <- th + theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())
  th
}
```

# Central Banks, Banks, Firms and Households

## Conventional Central Bank Policy {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
**Interest rates**

- Central banks mostly [target]{.marker-hl} interest rates through [very short-time] credit (overnight).

- The target is a [range]{.marker-hl} of auction results.

- Lower interest rates should cheapen investment, consumption, exports.
:::
:::{.column width=50%}
**Exchange rates**

- Appreciating a currency makes imports cheaper and exports more expensive.

- Exchange rates are targeted through supply-demand pricing, by releasing or buying up own [currency}{.marker-hl}.

- However, interest rate interventions also change the exchange rate, lower interest decreases demand for domestic assets and thereby domestic currency.
:::
:::

## Multiplicators of Central Bank Policy

Actual firm and consumer decisions are not very sensitive to short-term interest rates. Much investment is self-financed, consumption requires saved down payments.

Central bank policy can however be [effective]{.marker-hl} through [multipliers]{.marker-hl}, that is, someone else amplifying the effects.

## Bank Lending Channel {.smaller}

Banks are the main financing channel for firms that cannot afford to issue stock or bonds. Banks' decisions not to loan money are often the end of story.

- Central banks changing the lending environment leads to firms receiving funds that would otherwise have received zero funds (not more expensive loans).

- [Open market operation]{.marker-hl}: central bank buys securities from commercial bank, commercial bank earns less income on securities, has to lend more for revenue.

- Higher level interventions include changing regulation to make sure banks can continue loaning during financial contraction.

## Balance Sheet Channel (Credit Worthiness) {.smaller}

Monetary policy can also change the (apparent) credit-worthiness of households, increasing the credit available to them, and thereby consumer demand.

- Expansionary policy increases ([inflates}{.marker-hl}) asset values, which can be leveraged in loans.

- Lower interest rates decrease repayment burden, increasing profits, firm valuations and firm-related assets.

## Asset Price Channel {.smaller}

A fall in the interest rate increases ([inflates]{.marker-hl}) prices of stock and real estate. 

Fundamental stock prices are assumed to be the [present value]{.marker-hl} of future income minus credit cost, the latter factor decreases. 

On top of that, expectations of resale prices drive stock prices, which also increase when credit cost falls.

[Borderline]{.marker-hl} [investment]{.marker-hl} projects become profitable when credit cost decreases, increasing investment for these operations.

## Financial Crisis {.smaller}

In financial crisis, increased bankruptcies and opaque network effects decreases confidence in repayment, almost shutting off credit.

- This [shut off]{.marker-hl} the traditional policy channel for central bank policy.

- Unconventional monetary policy included [zero]{.marker-hl} [lower]{.marker-hl} [bound]{.marker-hl} policies, but also strategic purchases of [toxic]{.marker-hl} assets.

# Financialization

## Stockhammer 2010 {.smaller}

**Financialization** (in the economic sense): post-Fordist move towards credit- rather than income-fueled demand regimes after the [shareholder]{.marker-hl} [revolution]{.marker-hl}.

- Often, growth rates react positively on [aggregate demand]{.marker-hl}.

- Demand can be debt-financed if financial institutions and regulations allow for it: credit availability, credit worthiness and credit affordability.

- Banking norms, shadow banking, faster financial markets and liberalization decreased cost of and barriers to credit.

- Creates two growth model: [export-oriented]{.marker-hl} and [credit-financed]{.marker-hl}.

## Firms {.smaller}

For firms, increased access to financing comes with increased exposure to financial markets: [shareholder interests]{.marker-hl}.

- Shareholder interest is furthered by asset price inflation, prioritizing ["downsize]{.marker-hl} [and]{.marker-hl} [distribute"]{.marker-hl} over "retain and reinvest".

- Extreme case: Debt-financed stock buyback programs to increase stock value.

- Consequences: Crowd-out of investment and wages, studies suggest causal link.

## Households {.smaller}

For households, debt-financed consumption subsidizes income. (Housing) asset price inflation increase credit worthiness.

- Households increase borrowing, mainly mortgages, but also consumer credit and even payday loans.

- Allows for increase of consumption standards under stagnating incomes.

- Increases effective demand without increasing wage cost.

## Financial sector {.smaller}

**Financializtaion** challenges conventional central banking, creates more frequent [obstructions]{.marker-hl} of the policy channel.

- Increased importance of the less-regulated [shadow]{.marker-hl} [bank]{.marker-hl} [sector]{.marker-hl}.

- Key role as [lender]{.marker-hl} [of]{.marker-hl} [last]{.marker-hl} [resort]{.marker-hl}.

- Manage [structural]{.marker-hl} [deficiencies]{.marker-hl} (wage suppression and demand deficiencies) through consumer credit.

- Stabilize an increasingly unstable (*financial instability hypothesis*) and under-regulated (*financial liberalization*) economy.
